title: Timeouts and Backpressure
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and terminology of Timeouts and Backpressure.
Apply or interpret one Express.js 5 pattern related to application and upstream timeouts.
Identify a meaningful edge case and choose a repeatable local test for it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn timeouts and backpressure and connect the named syllabus points to a small Express.js example. The course baseline is Express 5.x on a supported Node.js LTS release; the page shows reference output, not execution of Node.js code.
content.why_it_matters: Timeouts and Backpressure matters because it helps keep the request/response contract explicit and the application maintainable as inputs, users and dependencies become less predictable. Measure before optimizing.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Timeouts and Backpressure is part of performance, concurrency, and scalability. Node handles I/O asynchronously, but CPU-heavy work can block the event loop. Measure latency and error rates, limit work, tune data access, control cache freshness, and design backpressure and shutdown behavior. For this topic, make the observable behavior explicit, then check what happens when an input is missing, malformed, unauthorized, or a dependency fails (choose the relevant cases for this lesson).

items.title: Application and upstream timeouts
items.text: Bound the request with a timeout, validate the returned shape and define an explicit failure policy. Retry only operations that are safe or protected by an idempotency mechanism.

items.title: Slow client behavior
items.text: Connect this syllabus point to Timeouts and Backpressure: state the expected behavior, identify a realistic edge case, and choose a test or observation that proves the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

items.title: Stream backpressure
items.text: Use asynchronous I/O for waiting work, but remember synchronous CPU-heavy functions still block the event loop. Bound concurrent work and honor cancellation, streams and backpressure.

items.title: Bounded work queues
items.text: Connect this syllabus point to Timeouts and Backpressure: state the expected behavior, identify a realistic edge case, and choose a test or observation that proves the behavior instead of relying on assumptions.

items.title: Preventing resource exhaustion
items.text: Keep the interface predictable for its client: use clear resource boundaries, explicit request/response formats, correct status codes, validation and tests for failure cases.

content_blocks.title: Read the example carefully
content_blocks.text: A useful way to study timeouts and backpressure is to start from the first syllabus point — application and upstream timeouts — and follow it through a small request or application example. Keep Express's built-in behavior separate from optional packages and your own application policy.

content_blocks.title: Worked example (reference only)
content_blocks.expected_output: A successful upstream JSON response produces a normalized status field; timeout/unavailable/malformed responses are handled explicitly.
content_blocks.notes: Use a real, documented upstream API in a lab. Do not hard-code credentials, retry every failed write, or trust a third-party response without checking its shape.

content_blocks.title: Safety / production rule
content_blocks.text: Module rule — Node handles I/O asynchronously, but CPU-heavy work can block the event loop. Measure latency and error rates, limit work, tune data access, control cache freshness, and design backpressure and shutdown behavior.

content.expected_output: A successful upstream JSON response produces a normalized status field; timeout/unavailable/malformed responses are handled explicitly.
content.task: Try it yourself: adapt the worked example to demonstrate timeouts and backpressure. Write down the exact request or command, expected status/body, one boundary case, and how you would reset the local lab. CodeLeaf does not execute Express code in this lesson page; run Node.js server examples locally.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example has a clear local run or inspection path and the required dependencies are named.
A normal request and a malformed/edge/failure request have documented expected outcomes.
No credentials, production data, or claim of successful runtime execution is included.
hints: Hint 1: identify which part of timeouts and backpressure is supplied by Express and which part belongs to your own application or another package.
Hint 2: check the official Express 5 guide/API reference and isolate the smallest example that proves one behavior.
Hint 3: verify a success case, a boundary case and the expected status/response; restart from a clean state before repeating.
content.solution_notes: Suggested approach: Node handles I/O asynchronously, but CPU-heavy work can block the event loop. Measure latency and error rates, limit work, tune data access, control cache freshness, and design backpressure and shutdown behavior. The sample is a focused reference fragment. Review all dependency, schema, proxy and runtime assumptions before using it in an application.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying an example without checking its assumptions
common_mistakes.why: A fragment may omit route setup, middleware order, external packages, database schema or production configuration.
common_mistakes.fix: State the runtime/dependency assumptions, run the focused example locally, and test a success path plus one failure path.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating all request values as trusted
common_mistakes.why: Parameters, query values, body properties, files and upstream responses can be missing or malicious.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate schema, type and bounds at the boundary; keep authorization and database constraints as separate checks.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the demo output means the server executed
common_mistakes.why: The course page shows reference output for Node.js/Express code; it is not an isolated Node runtime.
common_mistakes.fix: Run the example locally with the documented Node.js version and record actual command/output and test results.

summary: Explain the central idea behind timeouts and backpressure.
Connect the relevant subtopics to the request/response or application boundary.
Verify one normal outcome and one edge/error case with repeatable evidence.
run_instructions: Open a terminal in the lesson lab directory.
Install dependencies for the sample if required; use a supported Node.js LTS release.
Run the documented file with node, send the stated request with curl or an API client, and compare the actual status/body with the reference.
reset_steps: Stop the local process with Ctrl+C.
Clear only temporary/synthetic records or files created by the lab.
Restart the server before repeating the example.
troubleshooting: If node reports a module-syntax error, check package.json module type or use the matching CommonJS syntax.
If a package cannot be resolved, install the named dependency in the local lab and verify the lockfile.
If output differs, verify middleware order, the request path/method, environment variables and the expected runtime version.
